q6.answer: The server checks the format (pat_ plus exactly 32 allowed characters), computes SHA-256 of the full string and looks up the row by its unique token_hash, reading from the primary on every request with no cache. The row is usable only if Postgres, using its own clock, finds revoked_at null and expires_at later than now(). Otherwise, or if no row exists, the server returns the same generic 401.

q7.answer: Only a successful token-authenticated API call can change it. The lookup query also returns needs_touch, which Postgres sets when last_used_at is null or more than 55 minutes old, and the server runs the UPDATE only when needs_touch is true. That caps writes at about one per token per 55 minutes. There is no in-memory buffer.

q8.answer: The failure is logged and the API request is still served normally. needs_touch is still true on the next request, so that request tries the write again. The 1-hour bound breaks only if the write fails and the token is never used again.

q9.answer: Revoking sets revoked_at = COALESCE(revoked_at, now()) on the row. The row is kept for audit and nothing is deleted. Because the token is no longer active, it drops out of the list query and stops counting toward the 10-token limit, and its name becomes free again.

q10.answer: The UPDATE is scoped to id and the session user, so another user's token matches 0 rows and gets a 404, the same response as a token id that does not exist. An already-revoked token of your own still matches, and COALESCE keeps the original revoked_at, so the call is an idempotent no-op that returns 204. I did not decide whether 'already revoked' should get a different response.

q11.answer: If the COMMIT happened, an active api_tokens row exists. It counts toward the limit and holds its name, but nobody has the plaintext and the server cannot show it again. The browser says it could not confirm and reloads the list. If the name shows up, the user is told to revoke that token and create a new one; if it does not, they are told to try again. A plain retry hits name_taken, whose message explains the same recovery.
